back: Seven layers: how a forest feeds itself

A natural forest fills the space from the top branches to the roots.

Different plants use the light and moisture present at their layer.

A food forest imitates this pattern with productive plants.

The result is not one plant in one row, but many useful layers growing together.

Think of the crown of the tall tree, small trees, shrubs and soft non-woody plants.

Ground-covering plants protect it (the soil) on top, root plants grow beneath it, and climbing plants use suitable supports.

The height and spacing of plants depend on the plants and the site. These are planning layers, not fixed height bands.

A first Highveld example includes Wild Fig or pecan above lemon, naartjie and black mulberry.

You place Cape gooseberry and Wild Medlar together with vegetables, wild garlic, sweet potato and granadilla.

Take this as a planning example, not permission to plant all the species. Start by confirming which plant it is, frost tolerance, size when mature, and local restrictions.

Young plants need care during establishment: checking moisture, controlling weeds and protection from damage.

As plants grow, shade and fallen leaves change the conditions beneath them.

Check competition and access. Cut, make-small (thin) or adjust the planting of lower layers when what you see requires it; the system does not stop needing care on a fixed date.

back: Choosing plant species for South African food forests

Check the rainfall, frost, heat, soil and water availability at your site before choosing plants.

Mango can be damaged by frost. Quince needs a suitably cold winter in order to fruit reliably.

The name of a region or a protected corner suffices(?). Confirm each plant and each variety with a reliable local guide.

The first list includes pecan, walnut and indigenous fig; apple, pear, plum, black mulberry and loquat; rosemary, Wild Medlar, Cape gooseberry and Barbados cherry.

This list is not a recommendation for all of them. Check each plant against frost, soil, mature size and the local list of approved species.

Keep existing legal and project restrictions in force. Do not plant just from seeing a photo.

First examples for hot areas include mango, avocado, Natal Mahogany, banana, pawpaw, litchi, Wild Fig, Barbados cherry and Wild Dagga.

Marula, Mopane and baobab also appear in Limpopo examples. Suitability for your site still needs checking.

Useful trees are not automatically edible. Confirm which plant it is and its safe use; a landscape photo is not a guide for identifying food.

Indigenous plants suited to the site can support wildlife habitat as part of the design.

Choose by your site's ecology and the useful role of each plant. There is no percentage target with a source based on it in this lesson.

Protect existing natural vegetation. Do not convert healthy grasslands into a food forest just because the trees are useful elsewhere.

Establishing a food forest: observe and adjust

Start by checking the site, water supply and the available treatment. Protect bare soil early.

Temporary support plants can give shelter and useful cut material where suitable.

Main trees and lower layers can be added as conditions allow. Ground-cover plants do not want to wait for it to finish; avoid plants competing with young trees.

Start with the area you can water and maintain. Check existing plants before clearing.

Where suitable, plain cardboard under suitable mulch can reduce unwanted growth. Keep water able to enter the soil and leave tree trunks clear.

Plan spacing by the size of plants when mature. Prepare nursery plants for the next suitable planting window.

Look at how shade, roots and available water affect neighbouring plants.

Comfrey and wild garlic appear in a first underplanting example; check their suitability for your site before using them.

Cut or thin support plants when needed, using methods suitable for each species. Suitable clean cuttings can go back as mulch. Do not wait for a certain fixed year if competition is already damaging plants.

Choose the planting time when soil moisture and expected weather support establishment.

Rain can help, but check the root zone and keep a watering plan when the rain is [?nonsense word]. Avoid planting in waterlogged soil.

Check young plants after planting. Harvest time and inputs from outside depend on the species, site and treatment; there is no guaranteed harvest in the fifth year.

back: The three ethics: earth care, people care, fair sharing

Permaculture stands on three ethics. Earth Care means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems we must protect, not things to use up. People Care means the needs of your family come first, then the needs of your community. Fair Share means taking only what you need and returning the surplus - seed, food, water, knowledge - to the system.

These are not vague ideas. A farmer who sells all the eggs and vegetables but keeps nothing on the family table breaks People Care. A community that fences off a shared water source breaks Fair Share.

The ethics matter because they help you make decisions when there is no rulebook - when a neighbour asks to graze(?) cattle after a drought, or floods damage your swales (swale: a dug channel that catches rainwater). Build these three ethics into how you think before you build anything on the land.

Twelve design principles arranged as segments around a small seedling starting to grow in the centre, each shown with a simple picture - an eye for observing, a drop for catching water, a sun for energy, a circle for recycling waste.
Twelve principles: designing in harmony with nature

David Holmgren set out twelve design principles in the book Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison and David Holmgren together started the idea of permaculture. The three useful first places in this lesson are: observe and interact - look at your land for a full season before doing big earthworks; catch and store energy - notice rain, sun and biomass (living plant material such as grass and leaves) before they leave your site; and use edges and value the marginal - a fence line or a strip beside a road can be a useful place for watching.

Others you should know: produce no waste (food scraps become compost, compost becomes soil), use small and slow solutions (a bucket can water a bed without electricity), and use and value diversity. Hail damage to maize depends on the storm and the growth stage of the plant.

Choose two or three principles that speak to your biggest problem and apply them strongly. The others will become clear as you go.

back: Zones and sectors: organising your farm by energy

Zones and sectors help you reduce wasted work. Zones run from 0 to 5 according to how often you visit. Zone 0 is the house. In this example, Zone 1 is near the house and holds what you CHOOSE often - herbs, salad leaves. Zone 2 is the main garden and chicken area, visited once or twice a day. Zone 3 is the main field, visited once a week. Zone 4 is almost wild - fruit trees and livestock fodder needing attention occasionally. Zone 5 is left wild.

Sectors are energies coming from outside - sun, wind, rain, floods, fire. Look where strong wind comes from on your farm. Records from a nearby weather station can help you check where the wind comes from. Look where rainwater enters and flows over your land. Draw arrows (→) showing what you see.

Draw the zones and sectors on paper, and you will have a framework for your design.
